title: The Secret of Agnes's Signature
markdown:
The fog in Oakhaven was thick enough to butter toast, rolling off the canals like a sleepy grey cat. Perfect Midnight Bloom Club weather. Elara Meadowlight had her nose in moss on a damp canal wall, tiny lichen threads like miniature engineering. Finn Meadowlight, younger cousin and official action-man, tried to balance a half-eaten biscuit on his nose. It wobbled like a buttery ship.

“Elara,” he said, “are you sure Tilda said The Flour is Flying about the new receipt code? Sounds like a bakery cat with a sneeze.”

She looked up. “She was specific. Agnes Periwinkle’s receipts have a secret code. First clue: The Flour is Flying. Yesterday’s slip.” Greasy paper: sourdough, a dozen jam tarts, one enormous gingerbread man. 1.98, 1.75, 3.02. They did not add up to anything sensible.

Finn snatched it, thrilled. “Maybe the flour is flying. Whoosh. Clumsy baker.” He flung his arms and lost the biscuit to the cobbles, a sad end for pastry.

“Tilda isn’t clumsy. She’s particular. And she looked worried. She said we had to figure it out before the Serpent’s Scale Gang.”

The name made Finn’s eyes gleam. Rival children, bossy explorers, dramatic pronouncements, a habit of claiming the best climbing trees. Not villains. Competitive. Nosy.

“They wouldn’t want bakery receipts. They’d want maps. Or Extra-Cheesy Oakhaven Puffs.”

“Tilda thought they would.” Elara frowned. Their newest, quietest member was usually more interested in napkin-folding than chases. Tilda Buttercup had joined with an air of mystery, coat too large, voice too small, that was turning out to be merely peculiar.

They were due at the Lock Keeper’s Hut, hidden behind brambles and roses, secret knock three taps and a whistle. On the way they passed Agnes’s bakery: windows steamed, a gingerbread man in the display looking frankly enormous, and—Elara noted—the Serpent’s Scale Gang’s eldest pretending to study the price of buns while writing nothing down. Finn wanted to go in and ask for a tart. Elara steered him on. Damp wood, forgotten nets, old dreams. Sanctuary.

Near the hut the fog thickened, muffling horns and ducks. The allotment gate rattled under quick clouds. Then they saw her: Tilda silhouetted against a weak distant lamp, hunched as if trying to vanish into her own sleeves.

“Tilda,” Elara whispered. “You’re late. Did you solve it? Did Agnes leave jam tarts?”

Tilda wrung her hands, dry leaves on stone. “I’m sorry. I didn’t. It’s all my fault.”

Finn nudged. “She thinks the Gang has cracked it and ordered a hundred tarts.”

“No. Sillier.” Tilda bit her lip. “I can’t read very well.”

The fog seemed to hold its breath.

“Not properly,” she said, face raspberry-pink. “Not the numbers. I made up the code. The Flour is Flying is from a song my grandmother sang about her prize rooster. He’d flap like mad when she scattered flour. I thought it sounded like a good secret. The numbers are just numbers. Agnes writes them however she likes. I wanted to seem clever. Then I heard the Gang sniffing after secret meeting places, and I panicked. I didn’t want them to find the hut.”

Finn blinked, then grinned. “So there’s no code.”

Elara felt disappointment and understanding arrive together. Tilda had been trying to fit, with a song and a false puzzle. A gentler secret than any gang plot. Finn, who usually solved problems by moving, stood still long enough to look kind. A duck quacked in the fog, unimpressed with codes.

“So they’re just nosy kids who want our hut?” Finn said.

Elara remembered Agnes last week, apron floured, complaining about the postman while Elara sketched pigeons. If these numbers aren’t clear, I might as well send messages by pigeon. Agnes had traced each digit with an almost artistic flourish.

“Wait.” Elara pulled the crumpled duplicate. “Look. The ones are straight as soldiers. The nines are plump berries. The eights have loops like tiny spectacles.” Faded ink under her fingertip. Old paper. Canal damp. “It isn’t a code. It’s her signature. On every slip.”

“Just handwriting?”

“And she signs with care because she’s worried about recipes. A rival baker after her gingerbread spice. Locked tighter than a dragon’s hoard.” Elara’s mind raced. Last week Agnes had told the pigeons, and Elara, that even the postman could not be trusted with a parcel that smelled of cloves. The Gang had been asking questions—not about a hut. About the bakery. About which days the gingerbread men were still warm at four.

“They’re after the jam tarts and the gingerbread,” Finn said. “They think the code leads to the blend.”

Tilda’s eyes flickered hope. “Not after us?”

“After Agnes. And we know where she hides the book.” Elara pointed at the hut’s dusty shelves and tackle. “She told me, in confidence, the precious ones live in a locked box under the loose board by the old winch. She’d never tell a detective. Then she winked.”

The fog parted enough for a sliver of moon. The Gang were good at shouting discoveries. They had missed a baker’s flourish and a naturalist who knew her neighbours.

“Well then,” Finn said, already for the board. “Protecting to do. And Tilda—your secret’s safe. Next time try enthusiastic garden gnomes. Or a handshake with hopping.”

Tilda managed a real smile. The mist around her coat felt less like a hiding place. They lifted the board. The box was there, flour-dusted even in the dark, Agnes’s numbers shining on a tag in that same proud hand. Outside, someone crashed about in the brambles, bossy and late. Finn put the board back. Elara pocketed the receipt. The hut smelled of nets and old dreams and, faintly, gingerbread that was not theirs to give away. Tilda practised the secret knock under her breath, numbers not required. Finn ate the rest of a spare biscuit he had not balanced on his nose, as if that too were protection. Elara folded the receipt so Agnes’s eights still showed, little spectacles, wide awake. The brambles crashed once more, then gave up, and Oakhaven’s fog closed like a lid that knew how to keep a bakery secret.
characters: Elara Meadowlight (quiet child naturalist), Finn Meadowlight (a practical younger cousin)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic story for confident middle-grade readers
